sections.title: Overview
sections.text: OverviewA customer runs an enclave with no route to the outside world and wants AI inside it, kept running by their own people. Analysts need answers from documents that can never leave the enclave, and every model, index and package has to arrive through an approved transfer. The hard constraint is the boundary. Nothing crosses the enclave's network, artifact, identity or audit boundaries at runtime, so the system cannot fetch a model, a package or a telemetry endpoint when it needs one. A release that is missing one dependency has to fail before it is installed, not once it is live. The design splits into a connected build world and an offline runtime. Signing and a transfer staging zone are the only bridge between them, an offline registry is the one system of record for what can be deployed, and each release ships as a signed manifest that lists every artifact hash.

sections.title: 2. Clarifying Questions, Requirements, and Constraints
sections.text: 2. Clarifying Questions, Requirements, and ConstraintsSix Architecture-Changing Questions In this scenario, six questions shape the architecture more than all the rest: How is the data classified, and which handling rules follow from that? What compute hardware sits inside the enclave? How good must answers be, and how long can a person wait for one? What path does a software artifact follow to be imported, approved, scanned, signed and rolled in? Which identity system runs locally, and which storage and directory services can the application depend on? Inside the network, what limits apply to logging, retention, backup and disaster recovery? What each answer changes: Handling rules decide whether you may store document text, keep prompts, cache intermediate results, or write audit records that hold sensitive content. The hardware picks one of three shapes: a single smaller model, a bigger model with batching, or a workflow that leans on retrieval and pairs it with a light model. Quality and latency targets set the product's role: a tool that assists a person, a batch analyst, or a copilot that feels close to interactive. The import process sets how fast the customer can patch a vulnerability or refresh the model. Identity and storage decide whether you can plug into local SSO (single sign-on), file shares, object storage or authorisation backed by a directory. Logging and recovery limits settle two things. Can you see failures without exposing classified data? Can the organisation ride out a lost node or a lost site and still stay within policy? From Discovery to Requirements Once about half the questions have answers, stop chasing a complete picture. State your assumptions and turn them into requirements, kept in three lists: functional, nonfunctional and constraints. Functional requirements (what the system has to do): Package the model and services for offline use, so the whole runtime deploys with no internet connection. Sign and version every artifact, so each model, container and dependency traces back to an approved release. Run a local registry and a dependency mirror, so installs and redeploys never reach beyond the enclave. Integrate with local identity, so access follows the customer's approved accounts and groups. Provide observability, backups and restore procedures that work offline, so operations need no outside telemetry. Run an update and rollback ceremony that leaves an audit trail, so each promotion to production can be reviewed and undone. Nonfunctional requirements (how well it has to behave): Nothing depends on the internet at runtime. Installs from approved artifacts are reproducible. Every code file, model file and packaged dependency has provenance you can check. The system stays supportable when patches and model refreshes arrive only rarely. Constraints vs. Preferences A constraint is a wall the design must stay inside. Examples: all compute stays on-premises, logs are kept only locally, and updates arrive only through a manual approval path. A preference is softer, such as favouring one storage engine over another. Keep the two apart in your answer. Otherwise the team may optimise for convenience and break a boundary by accident. A Compact Interview Question Tree A small decision tree shows how you reason when facts are missing. Settling the hardest unknowns first tells the interviewer you are protecting delivery. MVP Prioritisation: Must, Should, Could The MVP (minimum viable product) must have: Offline packaging for the model and services. Signed, versioned artifacts. A local registry and dependency mirror. Integration with local identity. Offline observability and backups. An update and rollback ceremony that can be audited. The list is short on purpose. It is the least the system needs to be operationally credible on a controlled network. Could-haves include richer analytics dashboards, a choice of models, automatic canary releases and replication across sites. In an air-gapped setting they pull attention from the core problem. What the MVP Will Not Support Calls to a live model on the internet. Unmanaged package installs, or fetching dependencies on the fly. Agents that update themselves and skip the approved import process. Any promise of unlimited model size or of running arbitrary plugins. Any assumption that logs can go to a cloud observability stack. Backup as a vague promise. Every backup runs through a storage and restore path the customer has already approved. Naming these exclusions guards against scope creep and makes you look more trustworthy. Requirement-to-Component Traceability Map every requirement to a component. A requirement with no component behind it is a wish. Requirement Component or mechanism Offline model and service packaging A build pipeline that emits one deployable bundle holding the model, the service and the runtime assets Signed versioned artifacts Signing step, artifact registry, release manifest and a record of each promotion Local registry and dependency mirror A container registry on-premises, plus package mirrors for each language's dependencies Local identity integration A bridge to the directory or SSO, with role mapping and authorisation checks Offline observability and backups Logs and a metrics store kept locally, backup jobs, and checks that restores work Auditable update and rollback ceremony A workflow for approving changes, a ledger of releases and a rollback runbook No runtime internet dependency Network policy that denies egress, plus an allowlist of dependencies Reproducible installs Every version pinned, every manifest locked, and build inputs that never vary Verifiable supply chain Provenance records, signatures, scan results and evidence of approval Supportable under long update intervals Cautious dependency choices, compatibility checks and written restore paths The One Assumption to Protect First If you can defend only one assumption, defend the network boundary. The system has to work completely with no internet access at runtime. It shapes packaging, dependency management, model deployment, observability and rollback. If the customer relaxes it later, the design gets simpler. If you assume the reverse and are wrong, the whole architecture falls apart. Interview pointer: If the interviewer says "assume whatever you need", pin down the no-internet-at-runtime assumption first. I would expect an interviewer to check that one before any other. Why This Is a Strong FDE Signal The panel wants to see three habits at once. You care about the customer, you judge well as an engineer, and you deliver. Here that means finding the constraints that matter, prioritising while facts are missing, and keeping the solution shippable. You also guard the riskiest constraint rather than tuning the design to the easiest feature. What to say in the interview: ask the six questions: data handling rules, compute, latency and quality, artifact approval, local identity and storage, and logging and recovery limits. Turn the answers into the six must-haves listed above. Name the four nonfunctional requirements out loud. Finish with what the MVP leaves out.

sections.title: 3. Scale Estimates, SLOs, and Capacity
sections.text: 3. Scale Estimates, SLOs, and CapacityAnchor the Load Envelope to Customer Reality Candidates often slip on the first pass. They picture an on-prem service that analyses documents, guess at a few dozen active users, and settle on one model replica behind a queue. That holds up on an average day. Then the customer names a deadline (their busiest day, or a date by which the backlog must be gone) and the plan falls over. An enclave gives you little or no room to scale out later. Get the capacity plan right before anything ships. Start from how the customer really works. The case fixes four facts: 1,000 users, 20 QPS (queries per second) at peak, a corpus of 50 million pages, and a GPU pool that cannot grow. Those figures pick the architecture for you. The options are batch processing, online interactive extraction, or a split where indexing runs asynchronously under a smaller interactive layer. They also decide what failure looks like: a "slow response", or a "missed mission deadline". Keep four figures apart, since each answers its own question: Average load → describes ordinary daily behaviour. Peak load → guards you when bursts pile up in the queue. Growth → tells you whether the design lasts through a year of adoption. Headroom → stops you running on the brink of collapse when a large document lands. Storage Sketch Model weights and runtime packages, kept as one primary release and two versions you can roll back to. Vector or search indexes covering 50 million pages, with room for metadata and sharding overhead. Logs, audit trails and operational metrics, held for as long as the customer's local policy requires. glossary.definition: queries per second: How much traffic hits the system each second.
key–value: As in "KV cache": the model's memory of the prompt so far, reused so it does not recompute it for every new token.
service level objective: The target you commit to internally: "95% of answers in under 3 seconds".
large language model: The model that reads text and writes text — GPT, Claude, Llama. Powerful, but it will confidently make things up if you let it.
service level agreement: The promise to the customer, usually with penalties. Looser than the SLO, so you have room.
service level indicator: The actual measurement behind an SLO — latency, error rate, answer success rate.

sections.text: 4. Architecture and End-to-End FlowTwo Worlds Separated by a Controlled Update Path The clearest way to defend this design is to walk one request through it twice. On the first pass everything works. On the second, something critical has gone missing. Picture the scenario. Inside the restricted or classified network, a user submits a packet of documents. They want it classified, want fields pulled out of it, or want it redacted. The answer has to be useful and auditable, and producing it must not rely on the internet at all. One hidden constraint shapes everything else. Software, models and metadata reach the offline side through a single controlled update path and no other way. So we deliberately split the design into two worlds: an online side where things get built, and an offline side where they run. Nine Components in Dependency Order Present the components in the order they depend on one another, not the order they would sit on a slide: Connected build environment: gathers source code, pinned dependencies and model artifacts ahead of export. Artifact signing service: signs whatever bundle crosses the boundary and issues attestations that anyone can check. Transfer staging zone: holds each bundle in quarantine for inspection until the offline side admits it. Offline registry and package mirror: the one trusted local store for every approved model package, container image and library. Local orchestrator: runs canary rollouts, applies deployment policy and decides where services run. Model server: hosts the local model, or the inference runtime, that the document pipeline calls. Document pipeline: takes documents in, runs OCR/parsing, chunks them, retrieves context, scores, redacts and builds the final result. Local identity provider: confirms who each user and service is, without leaving the boundary. Local telemetry stack: collects audit events, logs, metrics and traces, and exports none of it. The main trust boundary separates the build environment, the only connected part, from everything else. Boundaries inside the enclave count too: orchestrator versus workloads, identity versus services, document pipeline versus telemetry store. Cutting the network link leaves untrusted code in place. It moves the threat model from internet exposure to admission control, least privilege and a strong audit trail. Top-Down Architecture Diagram Each box earns its place by meeting a requirement: Connected build environment → inputs that can be rebuilt identically. Signing service → evidence of exactly what crossed the boundary. Transfer zone → unvetted material never lands straight on the offline side. Registry and mirror → deployments stay deterministic. Orchestrator → keeps the runtime under management. Model server and document pipeline → do the actual work. Identity and telemetry stacks → every access is authenticated and every operation can be audited. System of Record vs. Cache vs. Queue This distinction separates a strong answer from an architecture that only looks good: System of record: approved packages and images live in the offline registry. User and service identities live in the identity provider. The audit log records each deployment and its time. Cache: model weights kept locally in memory, retrieval indexes or frequently used document fragments, and any response cache that saves repeating costly computation. Queue: jobs that ingest documents, tasks that scan, attest and export, and background jobs for enrichment or post-processing. External dependency: end-user traffic has none. The single thing from "outside" is the controlled build pipeline that produces the offline bundle. A frequent error is to let a cache act as if it were the source of truth. Air gaps make this worse. Nothing online refreshes it, so stale entries can linger unnoticed for a long while. When the registry marks an image as approved, the runtime must not quietly fall back to an older copy it has cached. A service credential revoked in the identity provider must be revoked everywhere, consistently, by the local control plane. Interview pointer: Interviewers often probe the split between system of record, cache and queue. For every component you draw, be ready to say which bucket it belongs to and what breaks once its data goes stale. End-to-End Happy Path Tell the happy path as a sequence of explicit state changes: Build from pinned dependencies. On the connected side, pin code, system packages and model package versions to known revisions. Scan, attest, sign, and export bundle. The bundle is checked for policy violations, given a provenance attestation, signed, then packaged ready for export. Inspect in the transfer zone. Before anything moves inward, the zone confirms integrity, policy conformance and chain-of-custody. Verify signatures offline. This proves that an authorised signer produced the bundle and that nothing altered it on the way. Import to local registry. The offline runtime can then pull approved model files, images and libraries from the local mirror. Deploy canary. The orchestrator runs a small share of model-serving and document-pipeline capacity against harmless test data. Run acceptance tests. They check authentication, ingestion of documents, latency, the quality of outputs, logging, and whether rollback is ready. Promote or rollback. A passing canary gets more traffic. A failing one is reverted, and its bundle goes into quarantine for review. Building, scanning, attesting, exporting and inspecting are all admin work, and they run asynchronously. In the live system, deployment, request handling and the inference users see are all synchronous. State it plainly to the interviewer. Document requests need a synchronous answer from the offline runtime. Updates and the supply chain run in the background, so a user never waits on them. Sequence Diagram of the Happy PathDependency-Failure Drill: Fail Closed Be ready to run this fail-closed drill, in which one transitive package is absent. When the package mirror lacks a dependency, the offline system must fail closed. It must never improvise by reaching across the boundary for the missing piece. Any unresolved dependency blocks promotion. The bundle stays quarantined in staging or the mirror until someone repairs the dependency and it is approved again. Backpressure and Flow Control Without backpressure, a burst of document uploads can melt an offline service. With it, the service stays stable. At ingestion: cap the number of concurrent uploads, check file size and type as early as possible, and queue oversized jobs rather than letting them grab parser resources straight away. At the pipeline: shard each document's work on a fixed key: case ID, tenant or document ID. Related state then lands in one place and retries behave deterministically. At the model server: limit concurrency, put a ceiling on batch size, and reject or defer work once GPU/CPU saturation passes a safe threshold. At the orchestrator: use rollout limits so the canary sees only a small share of traffic until acceptance tests pass. A good partitioning key keeps related work local and stops state from one document corrupting another. With document ID as the key, a retry or a partial failure is much simpler to reason through than when requests land on random workers. This counts most when a document's context, its redaction choices and its audit trail must agree. Component Responsibility Table Component Primary responsibility State ownership Notes Connected build environment Pin, package and compile artifacts ready for offline use Source tree and build metadata Sits outside the runtime trust boundary Artifact signing service Attest and sign artifacts Signing keys and provenance records Keep tight control over who can use the keys Transfer staging zone Examine each bundle before it is admitted Quarantine manifests Never serves runtime traffic Offline registry / package mirror Hand out approved packages and images Catalogue of approved artifacts The authoritative record of what may be deployed Local orchestrator Deploy services, scale them and roll them back Desired state and rollout state Applies policy on site Model server Run inference Model runtime state, cached weights Keep its API small and stable Document pipeline Ingest, analyse and redact documents, then assemble outputs Document processing state Usually the main request path Local identity provider Confirm who users and services are Identities, groups, tokens The authoritative record for access Local telemetry stack Store audit events, logs, metrics and traces Observability data Retain for as long as policy requires MVP vs. Later Evolution Keep the MVP (minimum viable product) small and opinionated. It needs one each of offline registry, orchestrator, identity provider, telemetry stack, model server and document pipeline, plus a clear canary process. Signing, verification and the transfer zone ship in the first release, because without them offline updates cannot be defended. What comes later: smarter scheduling, routing across several models, better retrieval, reindexing in the background and richer policy engines. Tell the interviewer you make the offline path dependable and auditable first, and only then tune throughput and make life easier for operators. Failure overlay to describe out loud: a bundle arrives, but the offline mirror lacks one transitive package. Promotion stalls in the orchestrator, which leaves the canary isolated. The telemetry stack logs the failed rollout. The registry holds the bundle in quarantine. An operator repairs the package on the connected build side and retries. Control Plane vs. Data Plane A diagram only helps if you can talk through how data, identity, state and failure move across it. Control plane: signing, verification, deployment, identity and policy. Data plane: inference and live document requests. Be clear about which workflows are synchronous and which are asynchronous, and about which system owns every durable state transition. In the job, this split lets you explain one architecture to customer stakeholders and engineering stakeholders alike. What the customer hears: "The system stays inside our boundary, and we can still take controlled updates." What engineering hears: "State has a known home, failures have a known edge, and promotion holds no surprises." 90-second interview summary: "I'd keep the connected build side apart from the offline runtime, with signing and staging as the only bridge. Inside the enclave sit a local registry, an orchestrator, a model server, a document pipeline, an identity provider and a telemetry stack. Requests are synchronous. Updates are asynchronous and tightly controlled. Deployable artifacts have one system of record: the offline registry. Local telemetry and the identity provider hold the audit trail. My biggest trade-off is security versus how hard updates become. The first production gate is simple: no bundle enters the enclave until it has proved, offline, that it is intact, complete and compatible. After that, a canary proves signature provenance, complete dependencies, working authentication and a rollback path before wider promotion."

    • At the pipeline: shard each document's work on a fixed key: case ID, tenant or document ID. Related state then lands in one place and retries behave deterministically.
    • At the model server: limit concurrency, put a ceiling on batch size, and reject or defer work once GPU/CPU saturation passes a safe threshold.
    • At the orchestrator: use rollout limits so the canary sees only a small share of traffic until acceptance tests pass.
  • A good partitioning key keeps related work local and stops state from one document corrupting another. With document ID as the key, a retry or a partial failure is much simpler to reason through than when requests land on random workers. This counts most when a document's context, its redaction choices and its audit trail must agree.

Component Primary responsibility State ownership Notes

Local orchestrator Deploy services, scale them and roll them back Desired state and rollout state Applies policy on site

Document pipeline Ingest, analyse and redact documents, then assemble outputs Document processing state Usually the main request path

MVP vs. Later Evolution
  • Keep the MVP (minimum viable product) small and opinionated. It needs one each of offline registry, orchestrator, identity provider, telemetry stack, model server and document pipeline, plus a clear canary process.
  • Signing, verification and the transfer zone ship in the first release, because without them offline updates cannot be defended.
  • What comes later: smarter scheduling, routing across several models, better retrieval, reindexing in the background and richer policy engines.
  • Tell the interviewer you make the offline path dependable and auditable first, and only then tune throughput and make life easier for operators.
  • Failure overlay to describe out loud: a bundle arrives, but the offline mirror lacks one transitive package. Promotion stalls in the orchestrator, which leaves the canary isolated. The telemetry stack logs the failed rollout. The registry holds the bundle in quarantine. An operator repairs the package on the connected build side and retries.
Control Plane vs. Data Plane
  • A diagram only helps if you can talk through how data, identity, state and failure move across it.
  • Control plane: signing, verification, deployment, identity and policy.
  • Data plane: inference and live document requests.
  • Be clear about which workflows are synchronous and which are asynchronous, and about which system owns every durable state transition.
  • In the job, this split lets you explain one architecture to customer stakeholders and engineering stakeholders alike.
    • What the customer hears: "The system stays inside our boundary, and we can still take controlled updates."
    • What engineering hears: "State has a known home, failures have a known edge, and promotion holds no surprises."
  • 90-second interview summary: "I'd keep the connected build side apart from the offline runtime, with signing and staging as the only bridge. Inside the enclave sit a local registry, an orchestrator, a model server, a document pipeline, an identity provider and a telemetry stack. Requests are synchronous. Updates are asynchronous and tightly controlled. Deployable artifacts have one system of record: the offline registry. Local telemetry and the identity provider hold the audit trail. My biggest trade-off is security versus how hard updates become. The first production gate is simple: no bundle enters the enclave until it has proved, offline, that it is intact, complete and compatible. After that, a canary proves signature provenance, complete dependencies, working authentication and a rollback path before wider promotion."

    return json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode("utf-8")

    value = mapping.get(key)

sections.text: 7. Delivery Plan, Observability, and Business ImpactFrom Prototype to Trusted Production A working demo is only the start. The milestone is the customer seriously asking when they can rely on it in production. Once that question lands, the interview moves past architecture into delivery. You now need a phased rollout, gates you can measure, named owners and a support model that holds up when the first incident hits. Inside an air gap, delivery belongs to the design itself. If the team must improvise to move, verify, install, watch or roll back the software, they have an encouraging demo they cannot deploy. The FDE's job is to turn the prototype into an operating path: safe enough for the enclave, dull enough for operators, valuable enough for users. Four Phases That Move Risk Out of the Dark Stand up a staging environment on identical hardware. Owner: infrastructure or platform engineering, with a security review by the enclave team. Exit criteria: trust roots, OS image, GPU/CPU profile, storage layout and node class all match production, so install and runtime results are representative. Why it matters: a staging setup built for convenience masks the problems that bite later, such as package incompatibility, driver mismatch, disk layout surprises and painful upgrades. Rehearse the signed transfer. Owner: release engineering runs it; security and operations watch the drill together. Exit criteria: the team carries a release bundle along the controlled transfer path, checks its signatures offline and installs it with no call beyond the boundary. Why it matters: real systems often fail at the transfer step. A plan of "someone will hand-carry it" falls short unless the handoff is written down, repeatable and auditable. Run a canary on a single node. Owner: operations runs it, while the product owner and an incident responder stay on call. Exit criteria: a single production node takes the new release, handles real traffic and stays within the agreed health thresholds for a set observation window. Why it matters: the canary contains the risk. No cloud-scale rollback shortcut exists on a closed network. So the first live node must show that configuration, dependencies, model and bundle behave well together. Keep a tested rollback bundle and its runbooks. Owner: operations carries out a rollback, release engineering keeps the artifacts, and the technical lead approves. 7. Delivery Plan, Observability, and Business Impact

From Prototype to Trusted Production
  • A working demo is only the start. The milestone is the customer seriously asking when they can rely on it in production.
  • Once that question lands, the interview moves past architecture into delivery. You now need a phased rollout, gates you can measure, named owners and a support model that holds up when the first incident hits.
  • Inside an air gap, delivery belongs to the design itself. If the team must improvise to move, verify, install, watch or roll back the software, they have an encouraging demo they cannot deploy.
  • The FDE's job is to turn the prototype into an operating path: safe enough for the enclave, dull enough for operators, valuable enough for users.
Four Phases That Move Risk Out of the Dark
  1. Stand up a staging environment on identical hardware.
    • Owner: infrastructure or platform engineering, with a security review by the enclave team.
    • Exit criteria: trust roots, OS image, GPU/CPU profile, storage layout and node class all match production, so install and runtime results are representative.
    • Why it matters: a staging setup built for convenience masks the problems that bite later, such as package incompatibility, driver mismatch, disk layout surprises and painful upgrades.
  2. Rehearse the signed transfer.
    • Owner: release engineering runs it; security and operations watch the drill together.
    • Exit criteria: the team carries a release bundle along the controlled transfer path, checks its signatures offline and installs it with no call beyond the boundary.
    • Why it matters: real systems often fail at the transfer step. A plan of "someone will hand-carry it" falls short unless the handoff is written down, repeatable and auditable.
  3. Run a canary on a single node.
    • Owner: operations runs it, while the product owner and an incident responder stay on call.
    • Exit criteria: a single production node takes the new release, handles real traffic and stays within the agreed health thresholds for a set observation window.
    • Why it matters: the canary contains the risk. No cloud-scale rollback shortcut exists on a closed network. So the first live node must show that configuration, dependencies, model and bundle behave well together.
  4. Keep a tested rollback bundle and its runbooks.
    • Owner: operations carries out a rollback, release engineering keeps the artifacts, and the technical lead approves.
    • Exit criteria: the last known-good bundle sits stored, tested and ready for immediate use, along with its escalation path, operator checklist, rollback steps and signatures.
    • Why it matters: treat rollback as a prepared artifact. When a release goes wrong, the team needs a trusted route back instead of a scramble to rebuild confidence under pressure.

    • Owner: security engineering or release engineering, whichever the local operating model assigns.
    • Alert threshold: treat any unexpected failure as a go/no-go blocker until the root cause is clear.
  • Model throughput and latency
    • Calculation: documents or pages handled per unit of time, together with request latency at the chosen percentile on user-facing paths.
    • Data from: local performance counters and service telemetry.
    • Owner: platform or ML (machine learning) operations.
    • Alert threshold: when latency leaves the band users accept, or throughput drops under the demand forecast, look at queue limits, hardware saturation, model quantisation or batching changes.
  • Capacity saturation
    • Calculation: how much of the safe operating headroom is in use, across token budget, queue depth, disk I/O, memory, GPU or CPU.
    • Data from: service queues and host metrics.
    • Owner: infrastructure or SRE (site reliability engineering).
    • Alert threshold: if the system runs close to its ceiling for a sustained period, scale up, shed load or throttle workflows before it turns unstable.
  • Mean time to repair
    • Calculation: the average time between declaring an incident and restoring service.
    • Data from: incident timelines.
    • Owner: incident management together with the primary on-call team.
    • Alert threshold: if repair times climb from one release to the next, the team probably lacks documentation, automation or spare capacity.
  • Release age
    • Calculation: time elapsed since the approved bundle now running was signed off and deployed.
    • Data from: deployment records and the release registry.
    • Owner: release manager.
    • Alert threshold: a release that is too old has drifted away from the latest security fixes and operational lessons. Releases that change too fast get too little soak time.

sections.text: 8. Interview Walkthrough, Trade-Offs, and PracticeMinute Zero: Open With the Customer Outcome Lead with what the customer gains, phrased the way they would say it: "We want local AI we can maintain inside an air-gapped government network. Updates have to be controlled, nothing can lean on the internet, and we need an audit trail that stands up to scrutiny." It shows you heard the operating constraint, and it keeps you out of a stock chatbot design. Before you draw anything, get the interviewer to confirm which boundary carries the most risk: What does the air gap protect? Is the isolation total, or do governed transfer points exist for media, packages and logs? Are we deploying into one secure enclave, several disconnected sites, or a staged network split into separate trust zones? Should analysts share one service, or do especially sensitive teams need their own isolated workstations? Spend minutes by risk, not by diagram size. Software ingress, provenance, identity and rollback deserve the most. Cosmetic model debates and over-tuned UI features deserve the least. Announce the plan out loud: "First I'll cover how software gets into the enclave and how we show it's safe. After that, we can walk the request path and how the team runs it." A 50-Minute Pacing Plan 0–5 minutes: discovery and constraints Give the customer outcome back in a single sentence. Pin down the air-gap boundary, how updates happen and what auditors expect. Ask who the users are, which document types matter and whether success means search, extraction, classification, summarisation, or all of them. Check where it runs: centrally, on analyst workstations, or both. Flag your riskiest assumption and promise to return to it. 5–10 minutes: scale and success criteria Estimate daily documents, typical size, peak concurrent analysts and freshness needs. Without given latency targets, state them in words: interactive queries feel quick; batch jobs may run slower. Track user adoption, offline install success, signature verification, release age and incident recovery time. Treat every capacity figure as illustrative until the customer confirms the workload. 10–18 minutes: architecture overview Sketch the trust zones: outside sits the build environment; a transfer gate links it to the enclave, which holds the admin plane, audit store, document pipeline, inference service, model registry and package repository. Keep the data plane apart from the control plane. Documents move inward; results and logs reach only approved destinations; nothing relies on cloud telemetry. No path ever breaches the identity, artifact or audit boundary. 18–28 minutes: trade-offs and system design decisions Bigger-model quality against hardware fit. Containers or virtual appliances. Update cadence against accreditation cost. A central cluster or workstations. Justify each by customer value and running cost, never taste. 28–35 minutes: security, provenance, and failure handling Cover signed artifacts, pinned dependencies and repeatable builds. Show a patch passing a controlled import gate and checks before promotion. Explain offline debugging with reproducible replay, health endpoints, structured event traces and local logs. Run the drill: new model weights, old index. What happens? 35–42 minutes: rollout and operations Walk through staging, the canary, rollback and user training. Say who owns each area: the platform, security, support and the analyst community. Show release age and approval gates lowering risk without freezing progress. Explain reuse in similar enclaves. 42–50 minutes: recap and follow-up defence Give the ninety-second version of the architecture. Point out the biggest trade-off. State the first production gate. Take questions; tie each answer back to boundaries, provenance or rollback. Trade-Off: Model Size vs. Hardware Fit This is usually the first tension interviewers probe. Extraction and summaries may improve with a bigger model. But it may not fit in local GPU memory, it answers slower, patching gets harder and the customer may have to buy or borrow hardware. A smaller model fits easily and is simpler to support, yet may struggle with noisy documents, specialised vocabulary or long-context reasoning. "Always biggest" and "always smallest" are both wrong. Optimise for the mission: For triage or structured extraction, a reliable, well-tuned small model can beat a brittle large one that is costly to maintain. Subtle legal or technical interpretation can justify bigger inference hardware, but only if enclave operators can sustain and safely patch it. Interview line: "I'd pick the smallest model that clears the quality bar on the customer's own documents. Each step up in size competes for enclave hardware, adds latency and adds accreditation work." Trade-Off: Containers vs. Virtual Appliances Containers give portability, repeatable deployment and cleaner separation of concerns. They fit an enclave with an existing platform team and components refreshed one at a time. A virtual appliance seals the stack in a fixed boundary with fewer moving parts, which some security teams find easier to review. The tension is operational complexity against governance simplicity: Pick containers if efficient scaling, controlled patching and reusable components rank highest. Pick an appliance if the customer prefers one tight, inspectable unit and slow, deliberate change. Let the organisation's existing standards decide. An existing hardened virtualisation standard favours the appliance. An existing secure container platform favours containers for upkeep and reuse. Trade-Off: Update Frequency vs. Accreditation Cost Frequent updates cut vulnerability exposure, lift model quality and speed feedback. Yet each one must be packaged, signed, transferred, verified, staged, tested and approved, and may trigger re-accreditation. "Ship weekly because we're agile" is wrong. Size the release train to the governance load the customer can carry: Keep urgent security patches on a separate track from new features. Prebuild trusted update bundles. Promote from dev to staging to the enclave. Make each high-friction change smaller, more predictable and easier to audit, so fewer are needed. Strong phrasing: "I'd favour fewer releases that we trust more. In an air-gapped setting, change costs you in engineering and in governance." Trade-Off: Central Cluster vs. Workstation Deployment One central cluster is easier to manage and observe, and every analyst reaches the same models. It suits many analysts on one service, where a managed platform is allowed. Workstations help on a heavily segmented network, at low volume, or when the capability must survive limited central infrastructure. Decide on user count, concurrency, isolation needs and how much central administration the customer can sustain. Workstations reduce reliance on shared infrastructure, at the price of harder patch distribution, more support and weaker consistency. A central service raises reuse and control, but becomes one operational asset to protect and monitor closely. If the enclave can host it, start central: governance and updates are easier there. Fall back to workstations for isolated teams or cut-off sub-enclaves. Interview pointer: The four trade-offs follow one pattern. Lay out both options, name the deciding factor in terms of the customer's real constraints, then commit to a default and say when you would leave it. Use the same pattern live for trade-offs this section does not list. Four Hard Follow-Up Questions "How do patches enter the network?" Via controlled import, never casual file copying. Builds happen outside the enclave; each patch is signed, scanned and packaged as an immutable release artifact. It crosses by a customer-approved transfer mechanism into a quarantine or staging repository inside the air gap. Before promotion, the enclave checks the signature and dependency manifests and runs regression tests. If pushed, split emergency security updates from planned releases. Emergencies still need provenance and validation but can use a faster approval path with pre-agreed criteria. Every crossing carries a named owner, a checksum or signature, and a promotion record. "With no cloud telemetry, how do you find faults?" On site, by design, with enough instrumentation that nobody guesses. The enclave keeps its own audit events, local metrics, health checks, trace correlation IDs and structured logs. Replayable fixtures from representative documents let you reproduce failures offline. Support flow: once an analyst flags a fault, record the index revision, document hash, model version, request context and involved service logs. You can then reproduce it with no data leaving the network. If policy bars full payloads, keep the smallest safe subset or a redacted reproduction bundle. Principle: disciplined internal observability plus rich release metadata replace external observability. "The weights changed but the index didn't. Now what?" It probes whether you see coupled artifacts. Version model and retrieval index together as a compatible pair. New weights that alter embeddings, tokenisation or ranking behaviour may force an index rebuild or revalidation. Index schema, embedding pipeline, prompts, tokeniser and model package form a single compatibility surface. A pure runtime gain behind the same interface may keep the index. A representation change needs a rebuild, or a parallel index staged to compare outputs before traffic moves. You show the unwritten contract between retrieval and generation, and a safe upgrade path rather than "updating the model." "How do you prove build provenance?" As chain of custody: where the artifact came from, which code built it, which dependencies went in and who approved its entry to the enclave. The evidence: artifact hashes, reproducible build steps, pinned dependency manifests, tagged releases or signed commits, plus a verification record at every hand-off. For detail, a build system emits attestations and policy checks verify them before install. Never claim absolute proof. You get strong evidence and a control you can defend. It ends the guesswork when an auditor or operator asks, "What exactly is running here?" Common Weak Answers and Repairs "Let's run our usual cloud stack on-prem." → Repair: name the cloud dependencies that would breach the air-gap boundary, and the enclave-local services that replace them. "Pick the largest model we can get." → Repair: tie the choice of model to what the hardware holds, the latency users accept and the cost of upkeep. "Security can handle the rest." → Repair: show that you own the artifact flow, identity, logs and rollback. "We'll patch monthly." → Repair: explain release trains, the emergency-fix path and the approval cost every update brings. "Logs can wait; we'll look when something breaks." → Repair: say what you must capture from day one so offline debugging is possible. "Model and index are independent." → Repair: admit that embedding behaviour, retrieval quality and index freshness have to stay compatible. To sound senior, drop the generic answer and say: "That works in plenty of environments. In an air-gapped enclave, though, the hard part isn't technical feasibility. It's managing change safely." Self-Scoring Rubric Discovery: Did you surface the customer's true outcome, where the boundaries sit and which unknowns are most dangerous? Estimation: Did you convey a sensible scale and capacity, and flag numbers as illustrative where needed? Architecture: Were the update flow, the trust boundaries, and the data and control planes each kept separate? Depth: Did you dig into the riskiest areas rather than give every box the same airtime? Security: Did you cover provenance, identity, transfer controls, logging and rollback, while admitting no control makes risk vanish? Delivery: Did you show the path from prototype through staged rollout to production support? Communication: Were you crisp and structured, and did you welcome redirection? Winning answers show judgement rather than box count: what matters, what can wait, what needs control and how the customer gains. The Final 90-Second Summary "I'd run document analysis inside the air gap as an enclave service under central management. Signed releases come in through a controlled import path. The model and index ship together as versioned bundles. Local observability lets us support it offline. On model size, I'd go as small as approved hardware allows while still passing the customer's quality bar on their documents. Accuracy matters, but so do hardware fit, update cost and accreditation friction. If the customer already runs a secure platform, I'd use containers. If governance simplicity comes first, I'd switch to a virtual appliance. My biggest risk is the tension between how often we update and how much review each update needs. A staged release train, signed artifacts and bundles we can roll back keep that in check. The first production gate: no bundle enters the enclave until it has proved, offline, that it is intact, complete and compatible. After that, an in-enclave canary has to show verified provenance, steady latency and a support runbook we've already tested." It works because it ties the design to the customer's goal, maintainable AI that runs locally and never crosses the enclave's network, artifact, identity or audit boundaries, and proves you can hold the design under pressure. Practice Assignments Solo exercise: Without looking at this page, write your own 90-second answer to this scenario. Then cut it again under one rule: a sentence stays only if it names a production risk, defends a trade-off or makes a boundary clearer. Pair mock: One person plays a sceptical security reviewer whose only questions are follow-ups on patches, provenance and logging. The candidate may say "secure," "robust" or "scalable" only if they define the mechanism behind the word straight away. Implementation exercise: Map the life of a single enclave update: commit the code, build, sign, stage, import, validate, promote and roll back. Flag each step that alters the audit log, the index or the model artifact. Then pick the exact step where you would halt the rollout if the weights changed and retrieval quality dropped. What to remember under interview pressure: when lost, come back to what the customer needs, where trust ends, how releases travel and how you undo one. Great FDE (Forward Deployed Engineer) answers are structured, carry believable numbers, stay safe without theatre, keep the customer in view and name trade-offs openly.

    • Is the isolation total, or do governed transfer points exist for media, packages and logs?
    • Are we deploying into one secure enclave, several disconnected sites, or a staged network split into separate trust zones?
    • Should analysts share one service, or do especially sensitive teams need their own isolated workstations?
  • Spend minutes by risk, not by diagram size. Software ingress, provenance, identity and rollback deserve the most. Cosmetic model debates and over-tuned UI features deserve the least.
  • Announce the plan out loud: "First I'll cover how software gets into the enclave and how we show it's safe. After that, we can walk the request path and how the team runs it."
A 50-Minute Pacing Plan
  • 0–5 minutes: discovery and constraints
    • Give the customer outcome back in a single sentence.
    • Pin down the air-gap boundary, how updates happen and what auditors expect.
    • Ask who the users are, which document types matter and whether success means search, extraction, classification, summarisation, or all of them.
    • Check where it runs: centrally, on analyst workstations, or both.
    • Flag your riskiest assumption and promise to return to it.
  • 5–10 minutes: scale and success criteria
    • Estimate daily documents, typical size, peak concurrent analysts and freshness needs.
    • Without given latency targets, state them in words: interactive queries feel quick; batch jobs may run slower.
    • Track user adoption, offline install success, signature verification, release age and incident recovery time.
    • Treat every capacity figure as illustrative until the customer confirms the workload.
  • 10–18 minutes: architecture overview
    • Sketch the trust zones: outside sits the build environment; a transfer gate links it to the enclave, which holds the admin plane, audit store, document pipeline, inference service, model registry and package repository.
    • Keep the data plane apart from the control plane.
    • Documents move inward; results and logs reach only approved destinations; nothing relies on cloud telemetry.
    • No path ever breaches the identity, artifact or audit boundary.
  • 18–28 minutes: trade-offs and system design decisions
    • Bigger-model quality against hardware fit.
    • Containers or virtual appliances.
    • Update cadence against accreditation cost.
    • A central cluster or workstations.
    • Justify each by customer value and running cost, never taste.
  • 28–35 minutes: security, provenance, and failure handling
    • Cover signed artifacts, pinned dependencies and repeatable builds.
    • Show a patch passing a controlled import gate and checks before promotion.
    • Explain offline debugging with reproducible replay, health endpoints, structured event traces and local logs.
    • Run the drill: new model weights, old index. What happens?
  • 35–42 minutes: rollout and operations
    • Walk through staging, the canary, rollback and user training.
    • Say who owns each area: the platform, security, support and the analyst community.
    • Show release age and approval gates lowering risk without freezing progress.
    • Explain reuse in similar enclaves.
  • 42–50 minutes: recap and follow-up defence
    • Give the ninety-second version of the architecture.
    • Point out the biggest trade-off.
    • State the first production gate.
    • Take questions; tie each answer back to boundaries, provenance or rollback.
Trade-Off: Model Size vs. Hardware Fit
  • This is usually the first tension interviewers probe.
  • Extraction and summaries may improve with a bigger model. But it may not fit in local GPU memory, it answers slower, patching gets harder and the customer may have to buy or borrow hardware.
  • A smaller model fits easily and is simpler to support, yet may struggle with noisy documents, specialised vocabulary or long-context reasoning.
  • "Always biggest" and "always smallest" are both wrong. Optimise for the mission:
    • For triage or structured extraction, a reliable, well-tuned small model can beat a brittle large one that is costly to maintain.
    • Subtle legal or technical interpretation can justify bigger inference hardware, but only if enclave operators can sustain and safely patch it.
  • Interview line: "I'd pick the smallest model that clears the quality bar on the customer's own documents. Each step up in size competes for enclave hardware, adds latency and adds accreditation work."
Trade-Off: Containers vs. Virtual Appliances
  • Containers give portability, repeatable deployment and cleaner separation of concerns. They fit an enclave with an existing platform team and components refreshed one at a time.
  • A virtual appliance seals the stack in a fixed boundary with fewer moving parts, which some security teams find easier to review.
  • The tension is operational complexity against governance simplicity:
    • Pick containers if efficient scaling, controlled patching and reusable components rank highest.
    • Pick an appliance if the customer prefers one tight, inspectable unit and slow, deliberate change.
  • Let the organisation's existing standards decide. An existing hardened virtualisation standard favours the appliance. An existing secure container platform favours containers for upkeep and reuse.
Trade-Off: Update Frequency vs. Accreditation Cost
  • Frequent updates cut vulnerability exposure, lift model quality and speed feedback. Yet each one must be packaged, signed, transferred, verified, staged, tested and approved, and may trigger re-accreditation.
  • "Ship weekly because we're agile" is wrong. Size the release train to the governance load the customer can carry:
    • Keep urgent security patches on a separate track from new features.
    • Prebuild trusted update bundles.
    • Promote from dev to staging to the enclave.
    • Make each high-friction change smaller, more predictable and easier to audit, so fewer are needed.
  • Strong phrasing: "I'd favour fewer releases that we trust more. In an air-gapped setting, change costs you in engineering and in governance."
Trade-Off: Central Cluster vs. Workstation Deployment
  • One central cluster is easier to manage and observe, and every analyst reaches the same models. It suits many analysts on one service, where a managed platform is allowed.
  • Workstations help on a heavily segmented network, at low volume, or when the capability must survive limited central infrastructure.
  • Decide on user count, concurrency, isolation needs and how much central administration the customer can sustain.
    • Workstations reduce reliance on shared infrastructure, at the price of harder patch distribution, more support and weaker consistency.
    • A central service raises reuse and control, but becomes one operational asset to protect and monitor closely.
  • If the enclave can host it, start central: governance and updates are easier there. Fall back to workstations for isolated teams or cut-off sub-enclaves.

Interview pointer: The four trade-offs follow one pattern. Lay out both options, name the deciding factor in terms of the customer's real constraints, then commit to a default and say when you would leave it. Use the same pattern live for trade-offs this section does not list.

Four Hard Follow-Up Questions
  • "How do patches enter the network?"
    • Via controlled import, never casual file copying. Builds happen outside the enclave; each patch is signed, scanned and packaged as an immutable release artifact.
    • It crosses by a customer-approved transfer mechanism into a quarantine or staging repository inside the air gap.
    • Before promotion, the enclave checks the signature and dependency manifests and runs regression tests.
    • If pushed, split emergency security updates from planned releases. Emergencies still need provenance and validation but can use a faster approval path with pre-agreed criteria. Every crossing carries a named owner, a checksum or signature, and a promotion record.
  • "With no cloud telemetry, how do you find faults?"
    • On site, by design, with enough instrumentation that nobody guesses. The enclave keeps its own audit events, local metrics, health checks, trace correlation IDs and structured logs.
    • Replayable fixtures from representative documents let you reproduce failures offline.
    • Support flow: once an analyst flags a fault, record the index revision, document hash, model version, request context and involved service logs. You can then reproduce it with no data leaving the network. If policy bars full payloads, keep the smallest safe subset or a redacted reproduction bundle.
    • Principle: disciplined internal observability plus rich release metadata replace external observability.
  • "The weights changed but the index didn't. Now what?"
    • It probes whether you see coupled artifacts. Version model and retrieval index together as a compatible pair.
    • New weights that alter embeddings, tokenisation or ranking behaviour may force an index rebuild or revalidation.
    • Index schema, embedding pipeline, prompts, tokeniser and model package form a single compatibility surface.
    • A pure runtime gain behind the same interface may keep the index. A representation change needs a rebuild, or a parallel index staged to compare outputs before traffic moves.
    • You show the unwritten contract between retrieval and generation, and a safe upgrade path rather than "updating the model."
  • "How do you prove build provenance?"
    • As chain of custody: where the artifact came from, which code built it, which dependencies went in and who approved its entry to the enclave.
    • The evidence: artifact hashes, reproducible build steps, pinned dependency manifests, tagged releases or signed commits, plus a verification record at every hand-off.
    • For detail, a build system emits attestations and policy checks verify them before install.
    • Never claim absolute proof. You get strong evidence and a control you can defend. It ends the guesswork when an auditor or operator asks, "What exactly is running here?"
Common Weak Answers and Repairs
  • "Let's run our usual cloud stack on-prem." → Repair: name the cloud dependencies that would breach the air-gap boundary, and the enclave-local services that replace them.
  • "Pick the largest model we can get." → Repair: tie the choice of model to what the hardware holds, the latency users accept and the cost of upkeep.
  • "Security can handle the rest." → Repair: show that you own the artifact flow, identity, logs and rollback.
  • "We'll patch monthly." → Repair: explain release trains, the emergency-fix path and the approval cost every update brings.
  • "Logs can wait; we'll look when something breaks." → Repair: say what you must capture from day one so offline debugging is possible.
  • "Model and index are independent." → Repair: admit that embedding behaviour, retrieval quality and index freshness have to stay compatible.
  • To sound senior, drop the generic answer and say: "That works in plenty of environments. In an air-gapped enclave, though, the hard part isn't technical feasibility. It's managing change safely."
Self-Scoring Rubric
  • Discovery: Did you surface the customer's true outcome, where the boundaries sit and which unknowns are most dangerous?
  • Estimation: Did you convey a sensible scale and capacity, and flag numbers as illustrative where needed?
  • Architecture: Were the update flow, the trust boundaries, and the data and control planes each kept separate?
  • Depth: Did you dig into the riskiest areas rather than give every box the same airtime?
  • Security: Did you cover provenance, identity, transfer controls, logging and rollback, while admitting no control makes risk vanish?
  • Delivery: Did you show the path from prototype through staged rollout to production support?
  • Communication: Were you crisp and structured, and did you welcome redirection?
  • Winning answers show judgement rather than box count: what matters, what can wait, what needs control and how the customer gains.
The Final 90-Second Summary
  • "I'd run document analysis inside the air gap as an enclave service under central management. Signed releases come in through a controlled import path. The model and index ship together as versioned bundles. Local observability lets us support it offline. On model size, I'd go as small as approved hardware allows while still passing the customer's quality bar on their documents. Accuracy matters, but so do hardware fit, update cost and accreditation friction. If the customer already runs a secure platform, I'd use containers. If governance simplicity comes first, I'd switch to a virtual appliance. My biggest risk is the tension between how often we update and how much review each update needs. A staged release train, signed artifacts and bundles we can roll back keep that in check. The first production gate: no bundle enters the enclave until it has proved, offline, that it is intact, complete and compatible. After that, an in-enclave canary has to show verified provenance, steady latency and a support runbook we've already tested."
  • It works because it ties the design to the customer's goal, maintainable AI that runs locally and never crosses the enclave's network, artifact, identity or audit boundaries, and proves you can hold the design under pressure.
Practice Assignments
  • Solo exercise: Without looking at this page, write your own 90-second answer to this scenario. Then cut it again under one rule: a sentence stays only if it names a production risk, defends a trade-off or makes a boundary clearer.
  • Pair mock: One person plays a sceptical security reviewer whose only questions are follow-ups on patches, provenance and logging. The candidate may say "secure," "robust" or "scalable" only if they define the mechanism behind the word straight away.
  • Implementation exercise: Map the life of a single enclave update: commit the code, build, sign, stage, import, validate, promote and roll back. Flag each step that alters the audit log, the index or the model artifact. Then pick the exact step where you would halt the rollout if the weights changed and retrieval quality dropped.
  • What to remember under interview pressure: when lost, come back to what the customer needs, where trust ends, how releases travel and how you undo one. Great FDE (Forward Deployed Engineer) answers are structured, carry believable numbers, stay safe without theatre, keep the customer in view and name trade-offs openly.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.text: Key Takeaways The boundary is the design, so hold every choice to one outcome: maintainable AI that runs locally and never crosses the enclave's network, artifact, identity or audit boundaries. Defend the no-internet-at-runtime assumption first, because relaxing it later simplifies the design while assuming the reverse breaks the whole architecture. Measure success with analyst turnaround time per case, which the customer can check from inside the enclave without trusting a vendor-reported figure. Size against the fixed GPU pool: 20 QPS (queries per second) at 2,000 tokens a request, 120 tokens a second per replica and 70% utilisation gives 477 replicas, a sign to challenge the request mix rather than ask for hardware. Split the design into a connected build world and an offline runtime, with signing and the transfer staging zone as the only bridge between them. Make the offline registry the one system of record for deployable artifacts, and never let a runtime fall back to an older cached copy. The first production gate is that no bundle enters the enclave until it has proved, offline, that it is intact, complete and compatible. Ship each release as a signed manifest that lists every artifact hash and declares every dependency, so a missing package fails validation before installation, not at runtime. A missing transitive package fails closed: promotion stops, the evidence is kept, the running release stays untouched, and a dependency-closure preflight prevents a repeat. Sort every failure into a policy: signature and authentication checks fail closed, a stale index degrades with a freshness warning, ingestion queues in a bounded buffer, and trust-root updates need a human. Keep every observability path local-first and approved, because a library that silently calls home is a leak. Version the model and the retrieval index as a compatible pair, since new weights that change embeddings or tokenisation force a rebuild or a parallel index. Roll out in four phases: staging on identical hardware, a rehearsed signed transfer, a one-node canary and a tested rollback bundle with runbooks. Pick the smallest model that clears the quality bar on the customer's own documents, because each step up competes for enclave hardware and adds latency and accreditation work. Favour fewer releases that you trust more, with urgent security patches on a separate track from new features.

Nothing at runtime touches the internet. Ship the model and the service as one offline bundle. The whole runtime installs from it and never calls out. Give every artifact a version and a signature. sections.title: Architecture explanation
sections.text: Architecture explanation Picture two worlds with a single controlled path between them. The trust boundary separates the connected build side from everything else. On the connected side, the build environment packs source code, pinned dependencies and model artifacts into a bundle anyone can rebuild, then exports it. A signing service attaches signatures and verifiable attestations to anything that will cross the boundary. The bundle then waits in a transfer staging zone. It sits in quarantine while we confirm its integrity, its chain of custody and its conformance to policy. Only then may it enter. Once inside, signatures are checked against the offline trust roots. Approved content goes into a local registry and package mirror, which become the offline source of truth. A local orchestrator runs the services and applies deployment policy. It also handles canary rollout, sending only a small share of traffic to a new release. The model server and the document pipeline do the work: ingesting documents, OCR (optical character recognition) and parsing, splitting into chunks, retrieving, scoring, redacting and building the result. A local identity provider and a local telemetry stack round out the enclave. No data leaves, and no cache is ever trusted over the registry.

sections.title: Rollout plan
sections.text: Rollout plan Week 0-1: agree the scope and write down the non-goals: no live internet calls, no fetching dependencies on the fly, no agents that update themselves, no cloud observability. Week 1-2: build a staging environment identical to production: same GPU profile, node class, OS image, trust roots and storage layout. Week 2-3: practise the full transfer and import drill. Verify signatures offline and install without any outside access. Week 3-4: write the handoff down so anyone can repeat it and audit it. "Someone will carry it over by hand" does not count as a process. Week 5: put a canary on one node with real traffic. It must stay within the agreed health thresholds for a set observation window. Week 6-8: build the rollback bundle as a proper artifact and test it. It holds the last known-good release, its signatures, an operator checklist and the escalation path. After pilot: add nodes only while install success, signature checks and capacity saturation stay healthy. Keep watching how old the live release is.

sections.text: Final 2-minute spoken answerI'd begin somewhere other than the model. In an air-gapped site, the boundary is the system design, not an extra limit bolted onto a normal AI system, so I argue every decision against it. I'd restate the goal as AI capability that runs and stays maintainable locally, without breaking the network, artifact, identity or audit boundaries. Every later choice gets tested against that line. The architecture is two worlds with one controlled path between them. On the connected side, a build environment collects model artifacts and pinned dependencies. Anything due to cross gets attested by a signing service. The bundle then sits in a transfer staging zone, quarantined and inspected. Inside the enclave, we check signatures against offline trust roots. Approved content goes into a local registry and package mirror, which is the source of truth. An orchestrator deploys a canary and the acceptance tests run. Only after that do we promote or roll back. Identity and telemetry stay inside, and nothing calls home. My named drill is a transitive package that is missing from the bundle. The system fails closed and blocks promotion. The current release keeps running, and the bundle goes to quarantine instead of anyone reaching outside to patch it. On capacity I'd be straight with them. A fixed GPU pool means the sizing formula soon gives an awkward replica count. The right move is to question the request profile and shift work out of the live path, not to request hardware that can never get in. My first production gate: a bundle proves offline that it is intact, complete and compatible, or it stays out.
